8 launch pads, 32 preparation zones: Satellite images confirm Russia built new drone base in 6 weeks

The facility near Millerovo could launch more than 100 jet-powered UAVs daily as Russia expands its long-range drone campaign against Ukraine.

Ashwin Shekhar

15 October, 2026 08:15 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Satellite imagery shows the area where a large drone launch site is under construction, near Millerovo, Rostov Region, Russia, 11 October, 2026 | 2026 PLANET LABS PBC/Handout via Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: News agency Reuters confirmed Thursday the assessment by Telegram OSINT channels that Russia completed construction of a major new attack drone facility in approximately six weeks.

The rapid construction comes as Russia expands deployment of jet-powered strike drones capable of reaching speeds of 600 km/h, posing fresh challenges to Ukrainian air defences.

Planet Labs imagery from 31 August, 2026 showed an undeveloped field near Millerovo in Russia’s Rostov region. Groundwork began the following day, with construction captured by the Copernicus Sentinel-2 and commercial satellites.

Show Full Article

By 11 October, Planet Labs imagery showed launch pads and buildings taking shape, while high-resolution Airbus and Planet Labs images from 12-14 October confirmed that the facility was nearing completion, with launch rails being installed.

The 0.9-sq km facility features eight launch pads and 32 preparation zones.

High-resolution imagery shows that physical launch rails have been erected on two pads, while guidance tracks are being installed at two others. The preparation zones would allow launch crews to fuel, programme and equip drones before deployment.

According to Ukrainian OSINT analysts, the facility’s layout closely mirrors that of an existing Russian jet-powered strike drone installation in Tsymbulova, in the Oryol region. The new site is just 3.5 km from Millerovo airbase, placing it within the air-defence coverage associated with the base, according to private threat intelligence firm DroneSec.

DroneSec analyst Mike Monnik told Reuters that the facility could support Russia’s deployment of Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones as part of a network of more than 11 strike locations across the country.

He warned that the speed of construction, combined with faster drones and gaps in NATO-provided counter-drone capabilities, could create significant vulnerabilities for Ukraine.

“The speed of construction demonstrates just how easily Russia can quickly deploy its already established offensive capabilities,” Monnik told Reuters . He added that the facility could launch more than 100 jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) a day, although actual deployments would generally occur in smaller waves.

Ukrainian forces have claimed that Russian deployments of jet-powered strike drones have reportedly increased six-fold over the past three months. Kyiv and surrounding areas have been among the principal targets as Moscow increasingly relies on jet-propelled systems to conduct strikes against Ukrainian territory.

Their higher speeds also complicate interception. Although relatively inexpensive interceptors costing less than $2,000 have been used against Geran-3 and Geran-4 drones, the long-term effectiveness of such systems remains uncertain.

The expansion of Russia’s drone capabilities comes amid a wider dispute over attacks on energy infrastructure and the role of US military assistance to Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump has urged Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian energy infrastructure ahead of a US-Russia diesel agreement, amid wider conflicts in West Asia.

In an interview with Financial Times published Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine had refrained from conducting deep strikes against Russian energy targets for three days, but Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure continued to intensify. He said Kyiv would continue targeting Russian oil facilities, claiming that Ukrainian strikes had taken between 40 and 50 percent of Russia’s capacity offline.

Zelenskyy also said he would agree to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in exchange for American Patriot air-defence interceptors, describing them as the “minimum” Ukraine would require. However, he said the response instead involved degraded Starlink services.

Ukraine separately reported a one-day restriction on SpaceX’s Starshield service which it said affected drone interceptions and strikes. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that the restrictions were imposed by US Central Command.

Ashwin Shekhar is an alum of ThePrint School of Journalism, currently interning with ThePrint.

(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)

Dasharatha’s dilemma: What economics Nobel teaches central banks about keeping promises

Dasharatha’s story in the Ramayana and Robert Hall & Michael Woodford's economic insights have a common lesson on promises and changing circumstances.

Bidisha Bhattacharya

15 October, 2026 07:42 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Images of Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford being displayed as they are announced as winners of the 2026 Nobel economics prize at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Sweden | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: “ Raghukul reet sada chali aayi, pran jaaye par vachan na jaaye .”

Every Indian familiar with the Ramayana recognises this well-known line from Tulsidas’s Ramcharitmanas, expressing King Dasharatha’s commitment to a defining principle of the Raghu dynasty: life may be sacrificed, but a promise must never be broken. For centuries, this unwavering reliability has been regarded as a cornerstone of righteous governance—a ruler who honours his word allows citizens to place their trust in his decisions and plan their lives accordingly.

Yet Dasharatha’s story also reveals the dangers of an unyielding commitment when circumstances change. This conflict between keeping promises and exercising judgement offers an understanding of the work of the two economists awarded the Nobel Prize for their contributions to understanding economic expectations and stabilisation. Their research helps explain why credible commitments are important for central banks, but also why credibility need not mean following a predetermined course of action regardless of what happens.

Show Full Article

Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University were recognised for their contributions to understanding the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. At the heart of their work is a deceptively simple idea: an economy is not a machine that responds predictably to policy interventions. It comprises millions of households and businesses that continually form expectations about the future. This means that those who can influence expectations about the future can, in turn, influence present actions.

Their work developed against the backdrop of the economic turbulence of the 1970s, when oil shocks brought high inflation and unemployment simultaneously, challenging conventional approaches to economic stabilisation. Rather than treating the economy as a system that policymakers could steer through immediate interventions alone, their research helped explain how individual decisions and expectations shape macroeconomic outcomes.

Also Read: Anne Carson is a literary Houdini. Her diabolical brilliance got her the Nobel

Living in tomorrow In 1978, Hall found an important insight in household behaviour. Building on Milton Friedman’s idea that families allocate spending based on anticipated lifetime earnings,

Hall envisioned individuals who incorporate all known future information into their current decisions.

Consider a young engineer in Patna who receives a job offer from a Bengaluru firm. Upon receiving the offer, she may begin planning for a motorbike or a flat rather than waiting for her first salary.

Hall’s research showed that, if families made decisions this way, current spending already reflects foreseeable future events and changes in consumption depend on new information that was not previously anticipated. Since genuinely new information is inherently unpredictable, consumption changes can, in this model, follow a pattern of random fluctuations, known in economics as a random walk.

This insight had important implications for economic policies: what people expect can matter as much as the immediate effects of a policy intervention. An announcement about future policy can therefore influence behaviour well before the government or central bank acts.

Woodford developed a broader theory of central banking centred on this forward-looking behaviour. Initially trained as a lawyer at Yale before transitioning to economics, he published his influential work ‘Interest and Prices’ in 2003. He examined how expectations about future monetary policy influence current economic decisions, including how businesses set prices.

Consider a dhaba owner who rarely updates his menu board. Knowing that he may not be able to revise prices immediately, he set prices today with anticipated future costs in mind.

Taken together, Hall’s work on household consumption and Woodford’s work on businesses showed that the economy is influenced more by public expectations about what policymakers will do over the next two to three years than current policy settings.

Woodford’s work consequently concluded that monetary policy primarily involves managing expectations, with a central bank’s communication serving as its most potent tool.

Following the 2008 financial crisis, when policy rates in several economies approached zero, central banks adopted his “forward guidance” strategy to commit to maintain low rates for an extended period. This commitment alone helped reduce borrowing costs and stabilise the economic recovery.

Dasharatha’s dilemma The Ramayana offers a cautionary message for central bankers. When Kaikeyi invoked the boons Dasharatha had granted her, demanding Rama’s exile, Dasharatha honoured his promise despite its devastating consequences. This part of the story shows that a promise made under one set of circumstances and fulfilled uncritically in another can become a liability rather than a virtue.

The lesson for central banks is that a commitment to an objective need not require inflexibility about the means of achieving it.

Central banks faced this challenge after the pandemic. The US Federal Reserve, having committed to keeping interest rates near zero for an extended period, faced constraints as inflation surged in 2021, delaying rate increases until March 2022.

This predicament had been foreseen by economists.

In a 2012 paper, Jeffrey Campbell and his colleagues at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago discussed what they called “Odyssean” and “Delphic” guidance. Odyssean guidance involves a binding commitment analogous to the Greek hero securing himself to his ship’s mast to resist the Sirens’ song. Delphic guidance, by contrast, refers to a sincere projection of the central bank’s responses to evolving conditions. Woodford was among the paper’s discussants.

The discourse has since resurfaced, with the Federal Reserve, under its new chair, reducing its reliance on inflexible guidance. Woodford argues that credibility comes not from following a predetermined path, but from consistently and reliably responding to unfolding events.

The wiser vow on Mint Road In 2016, India codified this philosophy into law by amending the RBI Act to establish a 4 percent inflation target with a tolerance band of two percentage points on either side. The framework also established a six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), with its decisions, voting records and minutes made public.

This framework marked its tenth anniversary this month, and the RBI’s decision on 7 October demonstrated its maturity. The repo rate increased by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent, marking the first hike since February 2023.

However, the most significant aspect was the adoption of a new stance termed “calibrated tightening.” This approach signals commitment and discipline rather than rigid adherence to a predetermined path. It signals to families and shopkeepers that the RBI will prevent an oil shock from shaping their expectations while allowing flexibility as data evolves. This reflects a blend of Delphic wisdom and steadfast resolve.

If Woodford were to meet Tulsidas, they might agree in a more nuanced interpretation of an enduring principle—an authority’s strength lies in the promise it is trusted to uphold, yet the most prudent course of action is not following a fixed path regardless of the circumstances.

The principle of “ Pran jaaye par vachan na jaaye ” holds, provided the vachan is judiciously chosen.

(Edited by Chingkheinganbi Mayengbam)

Brazil reduces workweek from 6 to 5 days. Businesses say will increase operating costs

The decision is a significant victory for President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who made workers’ rights a central part of his political agenda.

Sakshi Mehra

15 October, 2026 07:41 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Brazil President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva | Reuters/Carla Carniel

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Brazil has voted to give millions of workers more time away from work without losing pay. The country’s Senate approved a constitutional amendment on Wednesday, reducing the maximum working week from 44 hours to 40 hours and guaranteeing workers two days of paid rest each week.

The decision is a significant victory for President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who made workers’ rights a central part of his political agenda. It also comes less than two weeks before the 25 October presidential run-off against Right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.

However, while trade unions have welcomed the move, business groups warn that employers could face higher costs, with possible consequences for prices and jobs.

Show Full Article

“Those who work so hard to build Brazil also deserve to have time to live,” Lula said , celebrating the vote by highlighting what the change could mean for workers’ lives.

The amendment reduces the maximum working week from 44 hours to 40, while protecting salaries and guaranteeing two days of paid rest. It is intended to end the widely used six-days-at-work, one-day-off system, known in Brazil as the 6×1 schedule.

The change could benefit more than 37 million workers in the formal sector, according to government estimates. Under the new rules, businesses will have 14 months to adopt the shorter working week. It was approved by the Senate in two rounds of voting, with 75 senators voting in favour and one against in each round.

Also read: Economist went looking into Musk’s charitable avatar. And this is what it found

A regional shift The proposal also reflected a wider debate in Latin America over working hours. Chile has moved to a 40-hour working week, while Mexico is aiming for the same limit by 2030. Brazil’s decision places it within this regional shift toward shorter working hours.

Lula’s government has argued that shorter working hours can improve workers’ well-being without harming productivity. In January, Guilherme Boulos, head of the president’s General Secretariat, defended the proposal on similar grounds.

“When that worker is better rested, the result is that they will work better,” Boulos said , arguing that employees working six days a week may already be tired when they arrive at work.

Business groups have warned that reducing working hours without cutting wages could increase the cost of employing workers. Companies that need to maintain their current operating hours may have to hire additional staff or pay existing employees for overtime.

The National Confederation of Industry (CNI), which represents Brazil’s industrial sector, estimated in February that the change could increase annual employment costs by between 178.2 billion and 267.2 billion reais. It also warned that the burden could be particularly heavy for smaller businesses and the construction industry.

However, a study by Brazil’s Institute for Applied Economic Research (Ipea), published in February, estimated that the change would increase operating costs by less than 1 per cent in major job-generating sectors such as industry and commerce. It also pointed to the possibility of productivity gains and a large labour market.

(Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)
